newsitem.title: UK: Britain lends voice to Belarus concerns.
newsitem.headline: Britain lends voice to Belarus concerns.

text.p: Britain said on Thursday it had called in the Belarussian ambassador to "express concern" at the political crisis in the former Soviet republic.

Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko has drawn wide international criticism for his plans to hold a referendum this weekend on widening his powers and his refusal to compromise with parliamentary opponents.
"We are calling in the Belarus ambassador tomorrow morning to express our own concern at the political situation," a foreign office spokesman said.
Ambassador Vladzimir Shchasny would see Foreign Office Permanent Under Secretary Sir John Coles on Friday morning.
Diplomatic sources said it was relatively rare for a foreign envoy to be called in and the move was an indication of the extent of British disquiet at events in Belarus.
Lithuania, Ukraine and Poland on Wednesday issued a joint declaration calling for a constitutional resolution of the situation in Belarus and for human rights to be respected.
France and Germany have also protested, while Czech President Vaclav Havel on Thursday urged Lukashenko to pull back from the brink.

Prospects of a compromise between Lukashenko and his parliamentary opponents dimmed on Thursday after the Belarussian leader snubbed a Russian peace initiative, saying he was too busy to meet a delegation from Moscow.
Lukashenko, 42, who stayed away from talks with Russian parliamentary leaders on Wednesday, pressed ahead with his campaign for a referendum on Sunday to widen his powers.
Shchasny said he would attend Friday's meeting at the Foreign Office and would explain the reasons for Lukashenko's actions.
"I will try to describe the situation and explain the reasons for that situation," he told Reuters.
"I will try to explain that this is an internal affair and it will be settled by peaceful means."
A defiant Lukashenko declared on Thursday that he would not share power with anyone.
Lukashenko is seeking backing in a referendum for major constitutional changes which would extend his term of office by more than two years. He also wants parliament to abandon plans to impeach him.
Aides have indicated that Lukashenko could dissolve parliament and the consitutional court -- something he is not entitled to do -- if they try to unseat him.
